title: 04 — Parquet, Arrow and the Columnar Stack
html:
04 — Parquet, Arrow and the Columnar Stack

The one idea: Parquet is how columns are stored on disk: compressed, encoded and summarised, so readers skip what they don't need. Arrow is how columns are held in memory: one layout every engine shares, so data moves between tools without being converted. Together they are why a laptop can query hundreds of millions of rows.

1. What it is

Layer Standard Role SQL Server comparison
On disk Apache Parquet Columnar file format with encodings, compression and statistics Columnstore index segments
In memory Apache Arrow Columnar memory format, shared by engines without copying The batch-mode row buffers inside the engine
Over the wire Arrow Flight, Flight SQL, ADBC Move Arrow batches between processes and databases TDS, ODBC and JDBC, but columnar

The storage formats chapter introduces row versus columnar storage and what a Parquet file contains. This chapter goes deeper on encodings, statistics, the variant type, and the Arrow side.

2. Why it matters

  • Most query time goes to reading bytes. Encodings and pruning decide how many bytes you read.
  • Tables with semi-structured fields (vendor JSON payloads, document-extraction output) used to be either flattened by hand or stored as slow strings. Variant with shredding changes that.
  • Polars, DuckDB, Daft, PyIceberg and Spark all exchange data through Arrow. That is why moving a result from one to another is nearly free.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Inside a Parquet file

---
title: Parquet file — row groups, column chunks, pages, footer
---
flowchart LR
    F["Parquet file"] --> RG1["Row group 1<br/>(e.g. ~128 MB of rows)"]
    F --> RG2["Row group 2"]
    F --> FT["Footer<br/>schema, row-group metadata,<br/>column statistics, offsets"]
    RG1 --> CC1["Column chunk: isin"]
    RG1 --> CC2["Column chunk: nav_date"]
    RG1 --> CC3["Column chunk: nav"]
    CC2 --> P1["Dictionary page"]
    CC2 --> P2["Data pages<br/>(encoded, then compressed)"]
    FT -.-> IDX["Optional page index and bloom filters"]
  • Row group: a horizontal slice of rows. The unit of parallelism and of statistics-based skipping.
  • Column chunk: one column's values inside one row group.
  • Page: the unit of encoding and compression inside a column chunk.
  • Footer: the schema and per-row-group, per-column statistics (min, max, null count). A reader reads the footer first, then fetches only the chunks it needs.
  • Page index: optional per-page min and max, for finer skipping.
  • Bloom filters: optional, answer "is this value definitely not here?". Useful for high-cardinality equality lookups, such as one ISIN.

3.2 Encodings, then compression

Encoding Idea Best for
Dictionary Store each distinct value once, then small integer ids Low-cardinality strings (category, currency, rating)
Run-length (RLE) and bit-packing Store (value, count), and pack small ints into few bits Sorted or repetitive ids, booleans, levels
Delta encoding Store differences between neighbours Sorted integers and timestamps
Byte stream split Rearrange float bytes so they compress better Floating-point measures

Compression (Snappy, Zstandard, gzip and others) runs after encoding. Sorting data before writing makes runs longer and statistics tighter, which is why sort order and clustering matter.

3.3 Variant and shredding

Variant is a binary encoding for semi-structured values, defined by the Parquet project and adopted by Iceberg v3 and Delta:

  • A plain variant column is a Parquet group with two binary fields, metadata and value.
  • Shredding pulls frequently used fields into real typed columns (typed_value), keeping a binary remainder for the rest. Queries on shredded fields get normal column pruning and statistics.
  • Spark 4.0 and 4.1 can create and read VARIANT columns. Per the Iceberg blog, Iceberg 1.10 added variant reading on Spark 4.0, and Iceberg 1.11 added Spark 4.1 and writing shredded variant.
  • Shredding is available only in Parquet. Variant itself can also be stored in Avro and ORC.

3.4 Arrow, Flight SQL and ADBC

  • Arrow fixes how columns sit in memory (validity bitmap, offsets, values buffers). Two engines that both speak Arrow can hand over a table by passing pointers: zero-copy.
  • Arrow Flight is a protocol for streaming Arrow batches over the network. Flight SQL runs SQL over Flight.
  • ADBC (Arrow Database Connectivity) is a database API like ODBC or JDBC, but it returns Arrow. As of ADBC 24 (July 2026):
    • The Flight SQL, PostgreSQL and SQLite drivers are maintained by the Arrow project.
    • The Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery and DataFusion drivers moved to the independent ADBC Driver Foundry.

4. Working code

The script dictionary-encodes and run-length-encodes a sorted category column, compares it with plain text and zlib, then plans a query using row-group min and max statistics. Standard library only.

import json, zlib, random

random.seed(1)
# One column of a NAV table: SEBI category per row. Few distinct values, long runs when sorted.
categories = ["Large Cap", "Mid Cap", "Small Cap", "Liquid", "Gilt", "Flexi Cap"]
column = sorted(random.choice(categories) for _ in range(60_000))

plain = "\n".join(column).encode()
# Dictionary encoding: store each distinct string once, then small integer ids.
dictionary = sorted(set(column))
ids = [dictionary.index(v) for v in column]
# Run-length encoding of the ids: (value, run length) pairs. Sorted data gives very long runs.
runs = []
for v in ids:
    if runs and runs[-1][0] == v:
        runs[-1][1] += 1
    else:
        runs.append([v, 1])
encoded = json.dumps({"dict": dictionary, "runs": runs}).encode()
print(f"plain: {len(plain):,} bytes | dictionary+RLE: {len(encoded):,} bytes | "
      f"plain+zlib: {len(zlib.compress(plain)):,} bytes")
print("runs:", runs)

# Row groups with min/max statistics let a reader skip data without opening it.
nav_dates = [f"2026-10-{d:02d}" for d in range(1, 31)]
row_groups = []
for start in range(0, 30, 5):                       # six row groups, five days each
    days = nav_dates[start:start + 5]
    row_groups.append({"min": days[0], "max": days[-1], "rows": 5 * 2_000})

def plan(predicate_date):
    keep = [i for i, g in enumerate(row_groups) if g["min"] <= predicate_date <= g["max"]]
    return keep, sum(row_groups[i]["rows"] for i in keep)

for d in ("2026-10-23", "2026-11-02"):
    keep, rows = plan(d)
    print(f"WHERE nav_date = '{d}': read row groups {keep} ({rows:,} of {sum(g['rows'] for g in row_groups):,} rows)")

Output:

plain: 499,180 bytes | dictionary+RLE: 158 bytes | plain+zlib: 1,047 bytes
runs: [[0, 9807], [1, 10071], [2, 10053], [3, 10102], [4, 10079], [5, 9888]]
WHERE nav_date = '2026-10-23': read row groups [4] (10,000 of 60,000 rows)
WHERE nav_date = '2026-11-02': read row groups [] (0 of 60,000 rows)

What to notice:

  • 499,180 bytes of text became 158 bytes after dictionary and run-length encoding, because the column is sorted and has only six values. General compression (zlib) alone gets 1,047 bytes. Real Parquet does both: encode first, then compress.
  • The query for 2026-10-23 reads one row group of six. A date outside every range reads nothing at all.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Writing unsorted data. Statistics overlap, so nothing can be skipped, and runs are short.
  2. Thousands of tiny files. Each has a footer and its own row groups, and planning dominates the query time. Compact them.
  3. Very wide row groups for point lookups, or very small ones for scans. Tune for the workload.
  4. Storing JSON as a string column. Use variant (with shredding where supported) or real columns.
  5. Converting through pandas between Arrow engines. Stay in Arrow (to_arrow(), from_arrow()) to keep zero-copy.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

  1. Shuffle the category column before encoding, and compare the run count and the encoded size.
  2. Add a fourth "row group" whose date range overlaps two others, and show how overlapping ranges weaken pruning.
  3. If you have PyArrow, write the same column with pyarrow.parquet.write_table and inspect pq.ParquetFile(path).metadata.row_group(0).column(0) for its statistics and encodings.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does a reader fetch first from a Parquet file, and why?
  2. Why does sorting improve both size and speed?
  3. What does shredding add to a variant column?
  4. What does "zero-copy" mean between two Arrow engines?
  5. Which ADBC drivers moved to the ADBC Driver Foundry in 2026?

Answers

  1. The footer, because it holds the schema and statistics needed to decide which column chunks to read.
  2. Longer runs encode smaller, and tighter min and max ranges let readers skip more row groups.
  3. Typed columns for common fields, so they get normal statistics and pruning while the rest stays in binary.
  4. The second engine reads the same memory buffers directly, with no conversion or copying.
  5. Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery and DataFusion.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26 through web search.

  • Apache Parquet documentation: https://parquet.apache.org/docs/
  • Variant in Apache Iceberg: https://iceberg.apache.org/blog/variant-in-apache-iceberg/
  • Apache Arrow: https://arrow.apache.org/
  • ADBC 24 release: https://arrow.apache.org/blog/2026/07/28/adbc-24-release/
